title: Tenali and the Dream of Palace

full_text:
An opportunistic courtier named Subba Shastri, known for his greed, sought a clever way to enrich himself at the King's expense without doing any honest labor.

One morning, Subba Shastri arrived at the royal audience hall with an exaggerated look of pious awe. He prostrated himself before King Krishnadevaraya and exclaimed:
'Jahanpanah! Last night, a celestial vision blessed my sleep! You, our divine Emperor, appeared to me in a dream surrounded by golden angels, and with your own royal hands handed me a purse containing ten thousand gold dinars as a reward for my devotion!
Our ancient scriptures state that the dreams of righteous citizens are sacred omens. Therefore, I have come to receive the ten thousand gold coins you promised me in my dream!'

King Krishnadevaraya was taken aback. While he knew the courtier was scheming, he hesitated to dismiss the religious appeal openly, fearing he might appear irreverent before the traditionalists.

Seeing the King cornered, Tenali Raman stepped forward:
'Maharaj, Subba Shastri’s dream is indeed an extraordinary spiritual event. In fact, on that very same night, I had an identical dream!'

Subba Shastri grinned, assuming Tenali was supporting his claim: 'Thou seest, O King? Tenali confirms the dream!'

Tenali continued calmly:
'Indeed! In my dream, Maharaj, after giving Subba Shastri the ten thousand gold dinars, you fell into a deep financial crisis. Seeing your distress, Subba Shastri generously took out his own private family savings—twenty thousand gold dinars—and handed them back to you as an emergency loan to protect the empire!
He promised to deliver the gold to the royal treasury the very next morning!'

Subba Shastri’s smile froze. His jaw dropped in horror:
'What? I... I never dreamed such a thing!'

Tenali replied with razor-sharp logic:
'Why, friend Shastri! If the King’s promise of ten thousand coins in your dream is real enough to demand real gold from the treasury, then your promise of twenty thousand coins in my dream is twice as binding!
Pay the King the remaining ten thousand dinars right now, or confess that dreams are made of smoke and have no value in an honest court!'

Subba Shastri turned white as chalk, fell to the floor, and begged for the King's forgiveness, admitting that his dream was a greedy invention.
King Krishnadevaraya roared with laughter, dismissed the greedy courtier, and praised Tenali’s unmatched presence of mind, demonstrating that fictitious claims are best paid with imaginary debts.
moral: You cannot claim real wealth from an illusion; those who demand payment for dreams must be paid with phantom coins.
